description.en: The band low chest press uses resistance bands anchored at a low point. Pressing the bands up and forward in a decline-press-like path targets the lower pec fibers. The constant band tension and decline angle make it a strong lower chest builder for home training.

en: Anchor resistance bands at a low point on each side.
Stand facing away from the anchors with a band end in each hand.
Hold the bands at hip level with arms back behind your body.
Step forward to create band tension.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Press both bands up and forward at an upward angle until your arms meet at chest level.
Squeeze your chest at the top with arms extended.
Slowly return to the starting position with control.
Targets lower chest with bands
Constant band tension through the range
Useful for home training
Builds chest size and definition
Strong tricep engagement
No bench required

description.en: The barbell clean grip front squat is the standard front squat used in Olympic weightlifting, performed with a clean grip and elbows pointed forward. The bar rests on the front shoulders with fingers loosely under it. The position demands wrist mobility and upper back tightness while building quad and core strength.

en: Set up a barbell in a power rack at upper chest height.
Step under the bar with elbows up and palms facing the ceiling.
Let the bar rest across your front shoulders with fingertips loosely under it.
Stand up to unrack the bar and step back into your stance.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out.
Brace your core hard and keep your elbows pointed forward.
Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees, keeping your torso upright.
Drive up through your heels while keeping your elbows high. Lock out at the top.
Olympic lifting standard squat position
Forces upright torso and strong core engagement
Builds quad-dominant leg strength
Develops wrist and upper back mobility
Strong carryover to clean and jerk
Trains the rack position under heavy load

description.en: The barbell Kas glute bridge (popularized by trainer Kassem Hanson) is a glute exercise performed similarly to a barbell glute bridge but with a partial range of motion at the top. You lift only a few inches up and down, keeping the glutes under constant tension. It is a brutal glute pump exercise that maximizes time under tension at peak contraction.

en: Set up for a barbell glute bridge: lie on the floor with knees bent, barbell across your hips (use a pad).
Drive through your heels to lift your hips into a bridge position. Squeeze your glutes hard.
From the locked-out top position, lower your hips only 4 to 6 inches — a partial range.
Immediately drive back up to lockout. Squeeze hard at the top.
Continue with this short, controlled range. Do not return to the floor between reps.
Maintain constant tension on the glutes throughout the set.
Perform 12 to 20 reps per set. The pump will be intense.
Use moderate weight — quality of contraction matters more than load.
Maximizes glute time under tension
Brutal glute pump and burn
Trains the lockout position of hip extension
Easier to load than barbell hip thrust setup
Excellent finisher for glute workouts
Builds glute size and lockout strength

description.en: The barbell one arm snatch is a single-arm Olympic-style lift where you bring a barbell from the floor to overhead in one continuous motion using one hand. The unusual loading creates strong rotational and lateral stability demands while building explosive total body power. It is rare but excellent for athletic development.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, the barbell on the floor in front of you.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar in the middle with one hand.
Keep the other arm extended out for balance.
Brace your core hard and engage your lats.
Drive through your heels to start the bar moving up.
As the bar passes your hips, drop under it while pressing it overhead.
Lock out the bar overhead with one arm, knees bent in a partial squat.
Stand up to the lockout position. Lower the bar back to the floor with control. Switch arms.
Builds explosive total body power
Strong rotational and lateral stability demand
Unique loading pattern
Develops Olympic lifting skill unilaterally
Functional carryover to athletic movement
Time-efficient compound lift

description.en: The bent over shoulder pendulum is a shoulder mobility drill that uses gentle pendulum swings. The mover hinges forward with one arm hanging free and swings the arm in circles and back and forth. It is useful for shoulder warm-up and rehab.

en: Stand next to a sturdy support.
Place the non working hand on the support.
Hinge forward at the hips.
Let the working arm hang straight down.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Swing the working arm gently forward and back.
Then swing it side to side.
Finish with small circles in both directions.
Mobilizes the shoulder
Strong rehab drill
Useful warm-up
Builds shoulder range
Trains shoulder mobility

description.en: The bottle weighted deadlift uses filled water bottles or jugs as makeshift weights for the conventional deadlift. Holding a heavy bottle in each hand, you hinge and lift to train the entire posterior chain. It is a strong choice for home training when no barbell or dumbbells are available.

en: Fill two water bottles or jugs with water or sand for resistance.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, bottles on the floor in front of you.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bottles.
Pull your shoulders back and engage your lats.
Brace your core hard.
Drive through your heels to stand up with the bottles close to your legs.
Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
Lower the bottles back to the floor with control.
Trains the deadlift pattern with no traditional weights
Builds posterior chain strength at home
Easy to scale by changing bottle weight
Develops glute, hamstring, and back strength
Practical for travel or home training
Functional movement pattern

description.en: The Bulgarian split squat with a chair performs the standard Bulgarian split squat using a sturdy chair for rear foot elevation instead of a bench. It is the simplest at-home version of this effective single-leg exercise.

en: Place a sturdy chair behind you. Stand about 2 feet in front of it.
Reach your left foot back and place the top of your foot on the chair seat.
Stand on your right leg. Hands on hips or at your sides.
Lower your left knee toward the floor by bending your right knee.
Descend until your right thigh is parallel or your left knee is near the floor.
Drive through your right foot to rise.
Complete reps, then switch legs.
Ensure the chair is stable. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per leg.
At-home Bulgarian split squat with no gym
Builds single-leg strength
Uses common household furniture
Same benefits as gym BSS
Develops quad and glute strength
Exposes left-right imbalances

description.en: The cable decline press is a chest pressing exercise performed at high cable pulleys, pressing both handles forward and downward at a decline angle. The downward angle emphasizes the lower (sternal) head of the pectoralis major. The cables provide constant tension throughout, making it superior to many decline machine variants.

en: Set two cable pulleys at the highest position. Attach D-handles to each.
Stand between the cables facing forward. Grip both handles, palms forward.
Step forward into a split stance — one foot forward for stability.
Bring the handles to your shoulders with elbows bent and pointing back.
Press both handles forward and downward simultaneously at a decline angle.
Bring the handles together in front of your lower abdomen, squeezing your chest hard.
Slowly return the handles to your shoulders under control.
Maintain cable tension throughout. Brace your core.
Emphasizes the lower (sternal) chest
Constant cable tension throughout
Standing position adds core engagement
Easy to load progressively
Useful for breaking through chest plateaus
Different stimulus than decline machines

description.en: The cable lying regular grip curl is performed lying face up on the floor with a low cable behind the head. Using a shoulder-width underhand grip on a bar attachment, you curl through a strict bicep range. The medium grip provides balanced bicep stimulus while the lying position eliminates body english.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a bar attachment.
Lie on your back on the floor with feet near the cable station.
Grip the bar with an underhand grip at shoulder-width.
Extend your arms straight up over your chest with cable tension active.
Brace your core and press your back to the floor.
Lower the bar back toward your forehead by bending only at the elbows.
Continue down until the bar is near your forehead.
Curl back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
Strict bicep isolation
Lying position eliminates body english
Constant cable tension through the range
Balanced shoulder-width grip
Useful for hypertrophy training
Strong peak contraction

description.en: The cable twisting standing one arm chest press combines a unilateral cable press with a torso rotation. The lifter grips a single handle behind, presses forward, and rotates the torso through the press. The combo trains the chest and obliques together.

en: Set a cable to chest height with a single handle.
Stand facing away from the cable stack.
Grip the handle with one hand near the chest.
Set a staggered stance for stability.
Brace your core and set the hips facing forward.
Press the handle forward while rotating the torso.
Squeeze the chest and obliques at full extension.
Pull back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Combo chest and rotation move
Trains rotational power
Strong unilateral chest move
Builds the obliques
Strong cable move
Useful functional pattern

description.en: The decline diamond push-up elevates the feet on a bench while performing a diamond push-up with the hands forming a triangle directly under the chest. The decline angle adds upper chest involvement and the diamond grip nails the triceps. It is one of the toughest bodyweight triceps moves.

en: Place your feet on a sturdy bench or box.
Get into a push-up position with hands under the chest.
Form a diamond shape with the thumbs and index fingers touching.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward your hands.
Keep your elbows tucked close to your ribs.
Press through your hands to drive back up.
Lock out the elbows at the top.
Brutal triceps work
Hits the upper chest
No equipment beyond a bench
Advanced bodyweight move
Builds pressing strength
Strong tricep finisher

description.en: The donkey calf raise is a calf exercise performed bent forward at the hips with someone sitting on your lower back, or with a donkey calf raise machine or belt. The hip-flexed position puts the gastrocnemius under a deeper stretch than standing calf raises, creating a stronger growth stimulus. It was a favorite of Arnold Schwarzenegger.

en: Bend forward at the hips and brace your forearms on a bench or raised surface. Your torso should be roughly parallel to the floor.
Place the balls of your feet on the edge of a step, block, or weight plate. Let your heels hang below the step for a full stretch.
Have a training partner sit on your lower back (across your hips, not your spine), or use a donkey calf raise machine or weighted belt.
Let your heels drop as low as possible to feel a deep stretch in your calves.
Push through the balls of your feet to rise up onto your toes as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top for one to two seconds.
Lower under control over two to three seconds back to the deep stretch at the bottom.
Repeat for 12 to 20+ reps per set. The calves respond well to higher rep ranges.
Hip-flexed position stretches the gastrocnemius more than standing raises
Deeper stretch may drive greater muscle growth
One of Arnold Schwarzenegger’s favorite calf exercises
Builds the gastrocnemius heavily through full range
Easily scalable by adjusting partner weight or using a machine
Works with minimal equipment

description.en: The dumbbell incline close grip press variation is performed pressing two dumbbells together throughout the rep on an incline bench. The dumbbells stay touching as you press, forcing the inner upper pec and triceps to work harder. It is a strong choice for inner upper chest development.

en: Set a bench to a 30 to 45 degree incline.
Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand pressed together over your chest.
Hold both dumbbells with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Press the dumbbells together hard and keep them touching throughout.
Brace your core and pin your shoulders to the bench.
Lower the dumbbells together down to your upper chest.
Press the dumbbells back up while keeping them pressed together.
Squeeze the inner chest at the top.
Targets inner upper chest
Strong tricep involvement
Builds inner pec detail
Different stimulus than standard incline press
Useful for chest specialization
Strong stretch on each rep

description.en: The dumbbell incline T-raise is a shoulder isolation exercise performed lying face down on an incline bench, lifting both arms straight out to the sides (forming a T) with thumbs pointing up. The chest-supported position isolates the rear delts and mid-traps with no body english.

en: Set an adjustable bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie face down with chest on the pad.
Hold a light dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging straight down. Thumbs pointing up.
Brace your core. Press chest into the pad.
Lift both arms straight out to the sides until they reach shoulder height (T position).
Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout. Squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Hold for one second at the top.
Lower under control. Use light weight (5 to 15 lbs).
Repeat for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Builds the rear delts and mid-traps
Chest-supported position eliminates body english
Improves postural muscles
Excellent for shoulder balance
Easier to feel target muscles than standing T-raises
Useful for shoulder rehabilitation

description.en: The dumbbell lying one arm pronated triceps extension is a unilateral skullcrusher with a pronated palm down grip. The lifter lies on a bench and lowers the dumbbell across to the same side shoulder. The single arm work and pronated grip target the triceps from a unique angle.

en: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in one hand.
Press the dumbbell up over the chest with palm facing down.
Set the upper arm vertical pointing at the ceiling.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Lower the dumbbell across to the same side shoulder by bending the elbow.
Stop just before the dumbbell touches the shoulder.
Press back up to lockout extending the elbow.
Squeeze the tricep at the top. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong unilateral tricep builder
Unique angle
Builds arm symmetry
Trains the lateral head
Useful arm builder
Strong dumbbell move

description.en: The dumbbell lying row on rack is performed lying on your back under a rack or bench with dumbbells in each hand. By rowing the dumbbells up with elbows wide while lying down, you train the back from a unique angle that emphasizes the rear delts and rhomboids.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with dumbbells in each hand at chest level.
Position yourself under a rack or bench with the dumbbells alongside your body.
Plant your feet flat with knees bent.
Brace your core and press your back to the floor.
Row the dumbbells up by driving your elbows out to the sides.
Continue pulling until your elbows reach the floor.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back to chest level with control.
Unique back rowing angle
Hits rear delts and rhomboids
Lying position eliminates lower back stress
Builds posterior shoulder strength
Useful variation for back balance
Strong upper back engagement

description.en: The dumbbell lying single extension is a single-arm tricep extension performed lying on a flat bench. You lower a dumbbell toward your shoulder (or behind your head) and extend back up, one arm at a time. Training one side at a time exposes imbalances and allows focused tricep work.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in your right hand. Hold the left hand free or supporting your right elbow.
Press the dumbbell up to lockout above your chest.
Keeping your right upper arm vertical, bend at the elbow to lower the dumbbell toward your right shoulder.
Lower until your forearm is roughly parallel to the floor.
Extend back to lockout by straightening your elbow.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Keep elbow pointing to ceiling throughout.
Unilateral tricep isolation
Exposes left-right imbalances
Builds tricep size and strength per arm
Easy to load progressively
Simple setup
Great for arm symmetry

description.en: The dumbbell one-arm incline chest press performs an incline dumbbell press with one arm at a time. The asymmetric load demands core anti-rotation strength while building the upper chest unilaterally. It exposes left-right pressing imbalances.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie back with a dumbbell in your right hand at your right chest.
Place your left hand on your abs, at your side, or on the bench for support.
Plant your feet firmly. Brace your core hard.
Press the right dumbbell up to lockout above your chest.
Lower under control.
Fight the urge to rotate — maintain a flat back against the bench.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Use moderate weight due to asymmetric load. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Unilateral upper chest loading
Exposes left-right pressing imbalances
Builds core anti-rotation strength
Develops shoulder stability
Engaging variation for upper chest
Useful when only one DB is available

description.en: The dumbbell over bench reverse wrist curl with mat is a wrist extensor builder done with the forearm braced over a bench. The lifter holds the dumbbell with a reverse grip and curls the wrist up. The mat protects the forearm from the bench edge.

en: Place a padded mat over a flat bench.
Kneel beside the bench.
Hold a dumbbell with a reverse grip palm down.
Rest the forearm flat on the bench with the wrist past the edge.
Hold the wrist with the opposite hand for stability.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Curl the dumbbell upward by raising the back of the hand.
Squeeze the forearm hard at the top. Finish then switch sides.
Trains the forearm extensors
Strong wrist builder
Builds the forearms
Useful for grip
Builds wrist strength

description.en: The dumbbell overhead walking lunge is an advanced exercise where you walk forward in alternating lunges while holding two dumbbells locked out overhead. The overhead position demands extreme shoulder stability, core engagement, and total-body coordination. It is one of the most demanding lunge variations.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Press both dumbbells overhead until arms are fully extended. Lock them out directly above your shoulders.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders down and back. Stand tall.
Step your right foot forward into a lunge. Lower until your back knee is just above the floor.
Drive through your right foot to step forward into the next lunge with your left leg.
Continue alternating, walking forward while keeping the dumbbells locked out overhead.
Keep your core braced and the dumbbells stable. Do not let them drift forward or backward.
Use moderate weight — overhead stability is the limiting factor.
Builds elite shoulder stability and core strength
Trains overhead position under dynamic load
Develops total-body coordination
Builds the legs, glutes, and shoulders simultaneously
Excellent for athletes needing overhead stability
Time-efficient compound exercise

description.en: The dumbbell rear lunge (reverse lunge) steps backward into a lunge while holding dumbbells at the sides. Stepping backward is easier on the knees than forward lunges and maintains more tension on the front leg.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step your right foot back two to three feet.
Lower your right knee toward the floor.
Drive through your front (left) foot to return to standing.
Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side.
Keep torso upright throughout.
Use moderate weight.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per leg.
Knee-friendly lunge variation
Maintains tension on the front leg
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Easy to load progressively
Exposes imbalances
Simple setup

description.en: The dumbbell seated reverse grip biceps curl is a reverse curl performed seated on a bench. The seated position eliminates leg drive and forces strict form. The reverse (pronated) grip targets the brachialis and forearm extensors, building arm thickness and forearm size.

en: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing down (overhand grip).
Allow the dumbbells to hang at your sides at full arm extension.
Brace your core and stand tall through the torso.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending only at the elbows.
Maintain the reverse grip throughout the rep.
Squeeze the brachialis at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control to a full stretch.
Targets brachialis and forearm extensors
Builds arm thickness
Strict seated isolation
Different stimulus than supinated curls
Strong forearm involvement
Useful for arm specialization

description.en: The dumbbell sprinter thrust chest press is performed lying back on a bench with one foot planted on the floor and the other elevated like a sprinter at the starting blocks. The asymmetric stance creates a strong leg drive position for explosive pressing while the core resists the lateral force.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level.
Plant your right foot flat on the floor.
Place your left foot up on the bench beside your hip in a sprinter position.
Hold the dumbbells with palms facing forward.
Brace your core hard against the asymmetric stance.
Press both dumbbells straight up to lockout, driving with the right leg.
Lock out at the top with arms fully extended.
Lower the dumbbells back to chest level. Switch leg positions partway through the set.
Asymmetric stance creates explosive pressing power
Strong leg drive component
Builds chest, triceps, and front delts
Trains core anti-rotation
Different stimulus than standard pressing
Useful for athletic carryover

description.en: The glute ham single leg hyperextension is a hyperextension done one leg at a time on a hyperextension bench. The lifter hooks one foot under the pad and performs single leg back extensions. It builds the glutes and hamstrings unilaterally.

en: Set up on a hyperextension bench.
Hook one foot under the foot pad.
Let the other leg hang to the side.
Cross the arms over the chest.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Hinge at the hips to lower the torso down.
Drive the glute and hamstring to lift back up.
Finish then switch sides.
Trains each side
Builds the posterior chain
Strong unilateral move
Useful for athletes
Builds the glutes

description.en: The hanging knees to elbows is an advanced core exercise where you hang from a pull-up bar and pull your knees all the way up to touch your elbows. It is a CrossFit benchmark and one of the most demanding bodyweight ab exercises in any program. The full range of motion forces the lower abs and lats to work together aggressively.

en: Hang from a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats by pulling down on the bar.
Brace your core. Keep your body in a slight hollow position.
Initiate the movement by pulling your knees up toward your chest. As they rise, simultaneously pull yourself up slightly so your shoulders move back.
Continue pulling your knees up until they touch your elbows (or as close as you can get).
At the peak, your knees should be at your elbows and your hips should be fully flexed.
Lower your legs slowly under control back to the hanging start position.
If you cannot reach knees to elbows, work on hanging knee raises and hanging leg raises first to build strength.
Builds elite-level core strength
Trains the lower abs through full range of motion
Heavily engages the lats through the lat pulldown component
Improves grip and shoulder stability
Standard CrossFit benchmark exercise
Excellent test of relative core strength

description.en: The inverted chin curl with bent knee between chairs is a creative bodyweight biceps exercise. Pulling the chest to a bar across two chairs with a tight underhand grip blasts the biceps and lats.

en: Place a sturdy bar across two chairs about shoulder width apart.
Test the setup carefully to confirm it can hold your weight.
Lie face up under the bar with a close underhand grip.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor.
Brace the core and keep the back relatively straight.
Curl your chest up to the bar by bending the elbows hard.
Squeeze the biceps and lats at the top.
Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Builds biceps strength using only chairs and a bar.
Bent knees scale the difficulty.
Underhand grip targets the lats and biceps.
No spinal compression like with curls.
Develops grip and forearm strength.
Excellent at home biceps option.

description.en: The inverted row bent knee under table is a creative at home back exercise. Lying under a sturdy table with bent knees and rowing the chest to the edge builds the lats and upper back without weights.

en: Find a sturdy table that can support your full bodyweight.
Lie face up underneath with your chest below the edge.
Reach up and grip the edge of the table with both hands.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor.
Brace the core and keep the back straight from shoulders to knees.
Pull your chest up to the table edge by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row.
Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Builds back strength with only a sturdy table needed.
Bent knees make it accessible for beginners.
Trains horizontal pulling without spinal compression.
Strengthens the lats, mid back, and biceps.
Develops grip and core stability.
Travel friendly with zero special equipment.

description.en: The jump twist is a rotational plyometric exercise where you jump into the air and rotate your body 90 to 180 degrees before landing. It builds rotational power, core strength, and coordination. It is useful for athletes in rotational sports like golf, tennis, martial arts, and baseball.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, arms at your sides.
Dip into a partial squat and swing your arms to generate momentum.
Jump up while rotating your body 90 to 180 degrees in one direction.
Use your core to drive the rotation — not just your arms.
Land softly with bent knees, facing a new direction.
Immediately jump and rotate back to the starting direction.
Continue alternating directions for the desired number of reps.
Start with 90-degree rotations. Progress to 180 degrees as you build coordination.
Builds rotational power
Develops core strength through explosive rotation
Improves coordination and body awareness
Carries over to rotational sports performance
No equipment needed
Fun, engaging conditioning exercise

description.en: The kettlebell single front squat is a front squat with a single kettlebell held in the rack position on one side of the body. The asymmetric loading creates strong lateral force the core must resist while the front rack position emphasizes the quads and demands upright posture.

en: Clean a kettlebell to the rack position on your right shoulder.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, kettlebell resting on the front of your right shoulder.
Position your right elbow tucked at your side with the kettlebell against your forearm.
Brace your core hard against the asymmetric load.
Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees.
Keep your torso upright and resist tilting toward the kettlebell.
Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor.
Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps, switch sides.
Builds anti-lateral-flexion core strength
Asymmetric loading challenges trunk control
Front rack position emphasizes quads
Strong oblique engagement
Useful for athletes who need core stability
Reveals and corrects asymmetries

description.en: The kneeling scapular push-up is a beginner-friendly serratus anterior exercise. With straight arms in a kneeling push-up position, the shoulder blades retract and protract through full scapular range. It is excellent for building shoulder health and pressing stability.

en: Get into a kneeling push-up position with hands under shoulders.
Keep your arms straight throughout the entire movement.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to knees.
Allow your shoulder blades to squeeze together (retract).
Your chest will dip slightly toward the floor.
Push through your hands to spread the shoulder blades apart (protract).
Round your upper back at the top of each rep.
Move only the shoulder blades, not the elbows.
Strengthens the serratus anterior
Improves scapular control
Beginner-friendly version
Useful for shoulder health
Builds pressing stability
No equipment required

description.en: The leg assisted ring pull up is a regression of the strict pull up using rings set low. The lifter grips the rings overhead and uses the legs on the floor to assist the upward pull. The ring grip allows natural rotation while the legs scale the load.

en: Set gymnastic rings just out of reach overhead from a seated position.
Sit under the rings and grip them overhead.
Place the feet flat on the floor in front.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the chest up toward the rings using the legs to assist.
Bend the elbows and rotate the wrists naturally as you pull.
Squeeze the lats hard at the top.
Lower back down with control to the start.
Beginner friendly pull up
Builds the lats
Allows natural ring rotation
Useful pull up progression
Builds back size
Strong upper body builder

description.en: The lying knee roll over stretch is a gentle supine spinal twist where you lie on your back with knees bent and let both knees drop to one side while keeping shoulders flat on the floor. It mobilizes the spine through rotation, stretches the obliques, and decompresses the lower back. It is one of the most accessible spinal twists.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Extend both arms out to your sides at shoulder height in a T-shape.
Slowly lower both knees together to the right side, letting them rest on the floor.
Keep both shoulders pressed flat to the floor — your hips will rotate but your shoulders should stay grounded.
Turn your head to the left for a deeper twist (optional).
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Slowly bring your knees back to center, then drop to the left side.
Repeat 2 to 3 times per side.
Mobilizes the spine through rotation
Stretches the obliques and lower back
Decompresses the spine
Calming and restorative
No equipment needed
Excellent before sleep

description.en: The lying prone W to Y is a posterior shoulder activation drill. Lying face down, you transition from a W shape with bent elbows to a Y shape with arms overhead to fire the lower traps and rear delts.

en: Lie face down on the floor with the legs extended.
Lift the chest slightly off the floor.
Bring the arms into a W shape with elbows bent at the sides.
Squeeze the shoulder blades to hold the W position.
Slowly straighten the arms overhead into a Y position with thumbs up.
Squeeze the lower traps at the Y position.
Return to the W shape with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Activates the lower traps and rear delts.
Builds upper back posture.
No equipment needed.
Excellent warm up before pressing or pulling.
Improves shoulder blade upward rotation.
Reduces upper back stiffness.

description.en: Plank arm lifts (also called plank reaches) are a plank variation where you alternately lift one arm straight forward while maintaining a perfectly stable plank position. The arm lift creates a powerful anti-rotation challenge for the core, building elite trunk stability.

en: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart, body in a straight line.
Brace your core hard. Engage your glutes.
Slowly lift your right arm straight forward at shoulder height. Reach forward like Superman.
Keep your hips perfectly still. Do not let them rotate or bounce.
Hold for 1 to 2 seconds at the top.
Lower your right arm and place it back on the floor.
Lift your left arm in the same way. Continue alternating.
Move slowly. Anti-rotation control is the goal.
Builds elite anti-rotation core stability
Develops shoulder strength and stability
Trains balance under load
No equipment needed
Easy to scale by adjusting arm height
Useful for athletic core training

description.en: The quick feet run is an agility drill where the lifter runs in place with rapid short steps. The high turnover rate trains foot speed, calves, and conditioning. It is a key athletic warm-up and footwork drill used by sprinters and athletes.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Set the hands up in a running guard position.
Brace your core lightly.
Start lifting the feet off the floor in rapid alternating steps.
Keep the steps small and the turnover fast.
Stay light on the balls of the feet.
Pump the arms in time with the legs.
Continue the rapid foot speed for the working time.
Builds foot speed
Trains agility
No equipment needed
Strong cardio drill
Useful for athletes
Builds calf endurance

description.en: The roll thoracic spine lying on floor is a thoracic mobility drill. Lying with a foam roller across the mid back and extending the body back over it releases the thoracic spine and improves overhead mobility.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Place a foam roller across the mid back.
Cross the arms over the chest or place hands behind the head.
Brace the core lightly and keep the hips lifted.
Allow the upper body to fall back over the roller.
Press the chest open into thoracic extension.
Hold the extended position briefly.
Roll the spine slowly along the roller.
Mobilizes the thoracic spine.
Improves overhead mobility.
Useful for posture.
Reduces upper back tightness.
Joint friendly drill.

description.en: The seated in out leg raise on floor is a seated ab drill that combines a knee tuck with a leg extension. The continuous in and out motion loads the hip flexors and lower abs through a long range.

en: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and feet flat.
Place the hands on the floor behind the hips for support.
Lean back slightly with the chest up.
Brace the core and lift both feet off the floor.
Pull the knees toward the chest in a tuck.
Then extend both legs straight out.
Keep the feet from touching the floor.
Continue alternating for the working set.
Hammers the lower abs.
Trains the hip flexors.
Bodyweight move.
Builds the rectus abdominis.
Useful core finisher.

description.en: The seated pull up between chairs is a no-gym back move. The lifter places a sturdy bar across two chairs and sits underneath, then pulls the chest up to the bar. The seated start position scales the load and is great for beginners.

en: Set two sturdy chairs facing each other.
Place a strong bar or broomstick across the seats of both chairs.
Sit on the floor between the chairs under the bar.
Reach up and grip the bar with both hands at shoulder width.
Brace your core and keep the legs straight on the floor.
Pull the chest up toward the bar by bending the elbows.
Squeeze the lats hard at the top.
Lower back down with control to the start.
Beginner friendly pull up
No gym needed
Builds the lats
Easy at-home back move
Strong pull up progression
Builds bicep size

description.en: The standing calf raise is a single-joint isolation exercise where you rise up onto the balls of your feet by contracting the calves. Standing with knees mostly straight emphasizes the gastrocnemius (the larger, two-headed visible calf muscle), making it the foundational exercise for building calf size and definition. The bodyweight version is a great starting point that scales up easily by adding load.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart on a flat surface, or stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step or weight plate to allow a full stretch at the bottom.
Stand tall with knees mostly straight (a slight unlocked bend is fine). Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
If using a step, let your heels drop below the level of the step to feel a stretch in your calves.
Push through the balls of your feet to rise up onto your toes as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top for one second. Try to get your heels as high as your range allows.
Lower under control over a count of two to three seconds. If on a step, return to a deep stretch at the bottom.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a wall or pole for balance as needed.
Add load by holding dumbbells, wearing a weighted vest, or progressing to a calf raise machine.
Direct isolation of the calf muscles
Standing position with straight knees emphasizes the gastrocnemius
Easy to scale up by adding load
Highly portable — needs only a step or flat surface
Improves ankle stability and lower-leg endurance
Carries over to running, jumping, and athletic performance

description.en: The standing wring the towel is a forearm and shoulder mobility drill that uses a small towel. The mover grips the towel with both hands and twists the hands in opposite directions like wringing water out. It builds wrist and forearm mobility.

en: Grip a small towel with both hands.
Stand tall with the arms in front at chest height.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Twist one hand clockwise.
Twist the other hand counter clockwise.
Wring the towel as if drying it out.
Reverse the directions and continue.
Continue for the working set.
Mobilizes the wrists
Trains the forearms
Strong warm-up drill
Useful for grip
Builds the shoulders

description.en: The stick shoulder stretch is a classic shoulder mobility drill where a PVC stick is passed from in front of the body up and over to behind the body. The wide grip allows the shoulders to rotate through their full range. It is a staple warm-up move for Olympic lifters and shoulder rehab work.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a PVC stick in front of you with a very wide grip.
Keep your arms straight throughout the movement.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Slowly raise the stick up and over your head.
Continue passing it back behind your body.
Stop when the stick reaches your hips behind you.
Reverse the motion to bring it back to the front.
Improves shoulder mobility
Opens the chest
Useful for Olympic lifters
Great warm-up move
Helps reverse rounded shoulders

description.en: The suspender inverted row is a bodyweight back exercise using suspension straps. Hanging back with feet planted, you pull your chest up to the handles. The angle of your body determines difficulty, making it scalable for all levels. The neutral grip and free-moving handles add stability work to the row.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about waist height.
Grip the handles with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Walk your feet forward until you are leaning back.
Position your body in a straight line with arms extended.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Pull your chest up to the handles by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower yourself back down with control to a full extension.
Adjustable difficulty via body angle
Builds back strength with bodyweight
Strong core and stability engagement
No weights required
Suspension straps allow free-moving range
Excellent for home or travel training

description.en: The suspension trainer hamstring runner is a TRX hamstring exercise that combines a hamstring curl with a running motion. The lifter holds a hip bridge with feet in foot cradles and alternates curling each foot toward the hips. The alternating pattern builds hamstrings hard.

en: Set the suspension trainer foot cradles low.
Lie on your back and place the feet in the foot cradles.
Set the arms at the sides on the floor.
Brace your core and lift the hips up into a bridge.
Hold the bridge with the body in a straight line.
Curl one foot toward the hips by bending the knee.
Extend that leg back out and curl the other foot toward the hips.
Continue alternating curls in a running pattern.
Strong hamstring builder
Combo hamstring and glute move
Trains alternating control
Strong TRX move
Useful posterior chain finisher
Builds bridge endurance

description.en: The wrist roller is a forearm and grip exercise where you hold a horizontal bar with a weight hanging from a rope wrapped around it. By rolling the bar with alternating wrist flexion movements, you raise the weight up. It builds tremendous forearm endurance and is one of the best forearm exercises in any gym.

en: Set up a wrist roller — a short bar with a rope tied to the middle and a weight plate attached at the bottom of the rope.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold the bar horizontally with both hands, arms extended in front of you at shoulder height.
Begin rolling the bar away from you (overhand) by flexing one wrist down while extending the other up alternately.
Continue rolling until the weight reaches the bar at the top.
Reverse the motion: roll the bar toward you to lower the weight back down with control.
Maintain extended arms throughout — the work is in the wrists and forearms.
For variation: roll in the opposite direction (underhand).
Use light weight to start — your forearms will burn intensely.
Builds tremendous forearm endurance
Develops grip strength
Trains both wrist flexors and extensors
One of the best forearm exercises
Easy to load progressively
Useful for any grip-intensive activity
